messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Rivas, a 46-year-old European American graphic designer, described the trauma as beginning on an ordinary evening drive home when a patrol car appeared suddenly behind him, lights flooding his rearview mirror and siren cutting through the quiet road. He had done nothing wrong, he said, but the officer’s tone was sharp and insistent, and when Daniel was ordered out of the car he saw, in the glare of the cruiser, a man on the roadside with visible blood on his sleeve and a cut across his forehead from an unrelated collision nearby. That image stayed fixed in him: the authority of the police, the bright lights, the injuries on another person, and the sense that at any moment something could go horribly wrong without warning. In the weeks after, anything that reminded him of that scene—an unwanted thought of the stop, a glimpse of wounds or bandages on someone in the street, even seeing police near his office building—could bring back the full memory before he was ready for it. When it came back, he felt overwhelmed by emotion and often had to stop speaking entirely; at intake he would start to explain what happened and then lose the thread, as if the memory itself swallowed the rest of the sentence.

As the memory began intruding more often, Daniel came to believe that what had happened was not just frightening but deeply unfair and life-altering. He said it felt as though his life had been destroyed by something he could neither undo nor properly answer for, and the fact that no one had “made it right” left him angry and hollow. Those appraisals fed directly into his sense of danger: he could not relax even in his own home, because the experience had convinced him that safety was fragile and temporary. He described always checking escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, sitting in restaurants with his back to the wall and scanning for exits, and feeling his body stay tense and ready to react even during quiet evenings with his wife. The more he thought about how meaningless things felt now, and how unfair the whole event had been, the more his mind seemed to stay locked on the possibility of another sudden confrontation. In that state, police uniforms, flashing lights, and even small signs of injury on strangers became potent reminders; the presence of authority did not just recall the event but made him feel the same tightening in his chest and the same expectation that something bad was about to happen.

To keep those moments at bay, Daniel began spending long hours on his phone, gaming late into the night, and scrolling the internet while deliberately keeping his mind occupied all the time. He avoided other people whenever he could, turning down invitations and inventing reasons not to linger after work. For a while, those routines blunted the immediate distress, but they also meant he was alone with the memory whenever distraction slipped. A smell in the hallway, a passing siren outside his studio, or a sudden thought about being pulled over could break through the mental noise and bring the scene back with frightening clarity. Each time that happened, his body tightened again, and the effort to escape the feeling made him more vigilant about possible reminders in the environment. He found himself noticing police vehicles on his commute, scanning coworkers’ faces for visible injuries after casual weekend stories, and mentally mapping exits in every building he entered. The same habits that were meant to protect him seemed to keep his system on alert, and the more he used them, the more the reminders seemed to appear everywhere.

At work, Daniel’s graphic design projects had become harder to sustain because he was spending so much time trying not to think about the trauma that his concentration would break the moment an unwanted thought surfaced. He would disappear into screens at his desk, then miss parts of conversations with colleagues and withdraw from lunch breaks, which strained his relationship with others and made him feel even more cut off. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent afternoon when he saw a police officer standing outside his building beside a man with a bandaged hand; Daniel felt the old surge of fear, had to leave his workstation, and spent the rest of the day unable to settle. He came in saying he wanted relief from the constant tension and the sense that his life had been emptied out, but what he feared most was that one unexpected sight—or one more encounter with police—would pull him back under before he could ever feel normal again.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows negative appraisals increasing Daniel’s sense of danger, but it does not clearly say those appraisals lead to specific triggers/reminders appearing or becoming more salient.
The vignette describes maladaptive strategies being used to manage distress, but it does not state that the memory drives those strategies.
The vignette shows threat leading to heightened vigilance and repeated checking for reminders, but it does not clearly indicate that threat itself brings back the memory.
